plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected to the Weakness node representing CWE-522 via the EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship. Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, traverse MAPS_TO to find TaxonomyEntry nodes whose taxonomy is ATT&CK. Return the entry_id (ATT&CK technique/sub-technique ID) for each mapping.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, traverse HAS_MITIGATION to find associated Mitigation nodes. Return mitigation descriptions.

For each ATT&CK technique/sub-technique ID obtained from q2 (via the attack-technique-id join), retrieve the corresponding Technique or SubTechnique node and all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES. Return technique names, IDs, and mitigation descriptions.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected via EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS to the Weakness node representing CWE-287. Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.

For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all TaxonomyEntry nodes reachable via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK. Return the entry_id values (ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs) and the source AttackPattern ID.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes reachable via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation descriptions and the source AttackPattern ID.

Find all Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs supplied from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry join (q2). Return technique name, ID, and any parent Technique for sub-techniques.
For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q4, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES. Return mitigation name, ID, and the source technique ID.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected to the Weakness node representing CWE-294 via the EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, returning the entry_id values that correspond to ATT&CK technique identifiers.
Retrieve Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK identifiers obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings in q2.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the HAS_MITIGATION relationship.
For each Technique and SubTechnique node retrieved in q3, find all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

Even when the precise location of a targeted resource may not be known, naming conventions may indicate a small area of the target machine's file tree where the resources are typically located. CAPEC-101 (Server Side Include (SSI) Injection): An attacker can use Server Side Include (SSI) Injection to send code to a web application that then gets executed by the web server. Doing so enables the attacker to achieve similar results to Cross Site Scripting, viz., arbitrary code execution and information disclosure, albeit on a more limited scale, since the SSI directives are nowhere near as powerful as a full-fledged scripting language. Nonetheless, the attacker can conveniently gain access to sensitive files, such as password files, and execute shell commands.
CAPEC-470 (Expanding Control over the Operating System from the Database) has 1 ChildOf parent: CAPEC-66.

CAPEC-470 (Expanding Control over the Operating System from the Database) has 8 mitigations, named only as text: “Design: Follow the defensive programming practices needed to protect an application accessing the database from SQL injection”; “Configuration: Ensure that the DBMS is patched with the latest security patches”; “Design: Ensure that the DBMS login used by the application has the lowest possible level of privileges in the DBMS”; “Design: Ensure that DBMS runs with the lowest possible level of privileges on the host machine and that it runs as a separate user”; “Usage: Do not use the DBMS machine for anything else other than the database”; “Usage: Do not place any trust in the database host on the internal network. Authenticate and validate all network activity originating from the database host.”; “Usage: Use an intrusion detection system to monitor network connections and logs on the database host.”; “Implementation: Remove / disable all unneeded / unused functions of the DBMS system that may allow an attacker to elevate privileges if compromised”.
CAPEC-470 (Expanding Control over the Operating System from the Database) has Abstraction: Detailed; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: Very High.

CAPEC-470 (Expanding Control over the Operating System from the Database): An attacker is able to leverage access gained to the database to read / write data to the file system, compromise the operating system, create a tunnel for accessing the host machine, and use this access to potentially attack other machines on the same network as the database machine. Traditionally SQL injections attacks are viewed as a way to gain unauthorized read access to the data stored in the database, modify the data in the database, delete the data, etc. However, almost every data base management system (DBMS) system includes facilities that if compromised allow an attacker complete access to the file system, operating system, and full access to the host running the database.

plan.text: Retrieve all Techniques and SubTechniques under the 'Impair Defenses' Tactic (TA0008) and the 'Defense Evasion' Tactic (TA0005), together with every Mitigation that MITIGATES those techniques, so the analyst sees both the attacker actions that undermine controls and the defensive counters.

Retrieve AttackPatterns whose Category, description, or AlternateTerm relates to disabling, evading, or undermining security controls and defensive tooling, along with their Mitigations, Consequences, and ExecutionSteps, to give an abstract-level view of the attack and its defensive countermeasures.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

queries: MATCH (c:Campaign)-[:ATTRIBUTED_TO]->(g:Group) RETURN c.attack_id AS campaign_id, c.name AS campaign_name, g.attack_id AS group_id, g.name AS group_name LIMIT 100

MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 100

T1001.002 (Steganography): Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital messages that are transferred between systems. This hidden information can be used for command and control of compromised systems. T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares): Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SMB is a file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol for Windows machines on the same network or domain. Adversaries may use SMB to interact with file shares, allowing them to move laterally throughout a network. Linux and macOS implementations of SMB typically use Samba.

Windows systems have hidden network shares that are accessible only to administrators and provide the ability for remote file copy and other administrative functions. Example network shares include `C$`, `ADMIN$`, and `IPC$`.

T1027.003 (Steganography): Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital media such as images, audio tracks, video clips, or text files. Duqu was an early example of malware that used steganography. T1027.004 (Compile After Delivery): Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe(Citation: ATTACK IQ), csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.(Citation: ClearSky MuddyWater Nov 2018)

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a Phishing.

Windows systems have hidden network shares that are accessible only to administrators and provide the ability for remote file copy and other administrative functions. Example network shares include `C$`, `ADMIN$`, and `IPC$`.

T1685.005 (Clear Windows Event Logs): Adversaries may clear Windows Event Logs to hide the activity of an intrusion. Windows Event Logs are a record of a computer's alerts and notifications. There are three system-defined sources of events: System, Application, and Security, with five event types: Error, Warning, Information, Success Audit, and Failure Audit.

With administrator privileges, the event logs can be cleared with the following utility commands:

* `wevtutil cl system`
* `wevtutil cl application`
* `wevtutil cl security`

These logs may also be cleared through other mechanisms, such as the event viewer GUI or PowerShell.

Process hollowing is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Process hollowing is commonly performed by creating a process in a suspended state then unmapping/hollowing its memory, which can then be replaced with malicious code. A victim process can be created with native Windows API calls such as CreateProcess, which includes a flag to suspend the processes primary thread.

CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon): Operating system allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or users logon to a system. If adversaries can access these scripts, they may insert additional code into the logon script. This code can allow them to maintain persistence or move laterally within an enclave because it is executed every time the affected user or users logon to a computer. Modifying logon scripts can effectively bypass workstation and enclave firewalls. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or a remote administrative account may be necessary.

CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon) has Abstraction: Detailed; Status: Draft.

CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon): Operating system allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or users logon to a system. If adversaries can access these scripts, they may insert additional code into the logon script. This code can allow them to maintain persistence or move laterally within an enclave because it is executed every time the affected user or users logon to a computer. Modifying logon scripts can effectively bypass workstation and enclave firewalls. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or a remote administrative account may be necessary.

The smaller the attacker can make the space they need to search for the secret value, the greater their chances for success. There are a great many ways in which the search space may be reduced.”; “Explore 3 [Expand victory conditions] It is sometimes possible to expand victory conditions. For example, the attacker might not need to know the exact secret but simply needs a value that produces the same result using a one-way function. While doing this does not reduce the size of the search space, the presence of multiple victory conditions does reduce the likely amount of time that the attac…”; “Exploit 4 [Gather information so attack can be performed independently.] If possible, gather the necessary information so a successful search can be determined without consultation of an external authority. This can be accomplished by capturing cryptotext (if the goal is decoding the text) or the encrypted password dictionary (if the goal is learning passwords).”.

plan.text: Find the AttackPattern with id CAPEC-665 and retrieve all TaxonomyEntry nodes reachable via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, returning each entry_id (the ATT&CK technique/sub-technique id).

For each ATT&CK Technique or SubTechnique whose attack_id matches the ids supplied via the attack-technique-id join, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship, returning the mitigation name and id for each technique.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().has("id", within(ids)).project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Find all Techniques and SubTechniques that describe: (a) firmware modification or hiding (e.g., T1495 Firmware Hiding), (b) defeating, bypassing, or removing built-in authorization and verification checks on a hardware interface (e.g., T1542 Indicator Removal, T1070 Indicator Removal, T1542.001 Indicator Removal on Host), and (c) exploitation enabled by physical access to a machine (Tactic TA010 Physical). Include the parent Tactic for each so the analyst can see the high-level goal (e.g., Persistence, Collection, Impact).

For every Technique and SubTechnique returned by q1, retrieve the Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship, along with each Mitigation's description, so the analyst can see how a defender would stop each identified behavior.

Find AttackPattern nodes whose descriptions or ExecutionSteps involve firmware tampering, bypassing hardware-level authorization or verification mechanisms, or exploiting a physical-access vector to a device's I/O controller (e.g., Thunderbolt). For each matching pattern, retrieve its Mitigation nodes (via HAS_MITIGATION), its ExecutionSteps (via HAS_EXECUTION_STEP), and any TaxonomyEntry (via MAPS_TO) that links it to an ATT&CK technique, so the CAPEC-level narrative can be cross-referenced with the ATT&CK techniques from q1.

plan.text: Find the AttackPattern node with CAPEC ID 644 and retrieve all TaxonomyEntry nodes connected to it via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, returning each TaxonomyEntry's entry_id (the ATT&CK technique identifier).

For each Technique or SubTechnique whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK technique IDs supplied by the join, retrieve the technique/subtechnique node (name, id) and all Mitigation nodes connected to it via the MITIGATES relationship, including each mitigation's name and description.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Find Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose descriptions match the behavior of using stolen or purchased NTLM/LM password-hash values to authenticate to systems that trust legacy hash-based authentication, without the plaintext password (e.g., Pass the Hash, OS Credential Dumping, Valid Accounts, Use Alternate Authentication Material). Return technique IDs, names, and descriptions.

For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q1, retrieve all connected Mitigation nodes via the MITIGATES relationship, including mitigation IDs, names, and descriptions, so a defender can see how to stop each behavior.

Find AttackPattern nodes that MAPS_TO a TaxonomyEntry with taxonomy=ATTACK and entry_id matching the ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs returned by q1. For each matching AttackPattern, also retrieve connected Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION to surface CAPEC-level defensive recommendations.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

CAPEC-645 (Use of Captured Tickets (Pass The Ticket)) has Abstraction: Detailed; Likelihood_Of_Attack: Low; Status: Stable; Typical_Severity: High.

CAPEC-645 (Use of Captured Tickets (Pass The Ticket)): An adversary uses stolen Kerberos tickets to access systems/resources that leverage the Kerberos authentication protocol. The Kerberos authentication protocol centers around a ticketing system which is used to request/grant access to services and to then access the requested services. An adversary can obtain any one of these tickets (e.g. Service Ticket, Ticket Granting Ticket, Silver Ticket, or Golden Ticket) to authenticate to a system/resource without needing the account's credentials. Depending on the ticket obtained, the adversary may be able to access a particular resource or generate TGTs for any account within an Active Directory Domain.

T1550.003 (Pass the Ticket) description: Adversaries may “pass the ticket” using stolen Kerberos tickets to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls. Pass the ticket (PtT) is a method of authenticating to a system using Kerberos tickets without having access to an account's password. Kerberos authentication can be used as the first step to lateral movement to a remote system.

When preforming PtT, valid Kerberos tickets for [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) are captured by [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003). A user's service tickets or ticket granting ticket (TGT) may be obtained, depending on the level of access. A service ticket allows for access to a particular resource, whereas a TGT can be used to request service tickets from the Ticket Granting Service (TGS) to access any resource the user has privileges to access.(Citation: ADSecurity AD Kerberos Attacks)(Citation: GentilKiwi Pass the Ticket)

A [Silver Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/002) can be obtained for services that use Kerberos as an authentication mechanism and are used to generate tickets to access that particular resource and the system that hosts the resource (e.g., SharePoint).(Citation: ADSecurity AD Kerberos Attacks)

A [Golden Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/001) can be obtained for the domain using the Key Distribution Service account KRBTGT account NTLM hash, which enables generation of TGTs for any account in Active Directory.(Citation: Campbell 2014)

Adversaries may also create a valid Kerberos ticket using other user information, such as stolen password hashes or AES keys. For example, "overpassing the hash" involves using a NTLM password hash to authenticate as a user (i.e. [Pass the Hash](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002)) while also using the password hash to create a valid Kerberos ticket.(Citation: Stealthbits Overpass-the-Hash).

Find Techniques and SubTechniques that describe social-engineering or impersonation-based credential harvesting (e.g. an attacker posing as a trusted business contact to elicit login credentials or other confidential data). For each matching Technique or SubTechnique, retrieve the Tactic(s) it falls under via the HAS_TACTIC relationship, so the broad intrusion phase(s) can be identified.

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

gold_question: Which ATT&CK tactics do the techniques mapped from CAPEC-565 (Password Spraying) belong to?
note: built entirely from the description of cycling common passwords across many accounts

plan.text: Find AttackPattern nodes whose description matches: an attacker tries a short list of commonly used passwords against many different user accounts, moving to the next account before repeating any password, in order to discover valid credentials (i.e., password spraying / credential stuffing / password guessing across accounts). For each matching AttackPattern, also retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry where taxonomy is ATTACK, to obtain the ATT&CK technique id for joining. Include ExecutionStep and Prerequisite nodes to confirm the cycling-across-accounts flow.

For each ATT&CK Technique or SubTechnique identified via the join (attack-technique-id), retrieve the Tactic node(s) it belongs to (i.e., the broad phase of the intrusion such as Initial Access, Credential Access, etc.). Return the Tactic name and id for each matched technique.

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

For each matching pattern, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry where the taxonomy is ATT&CK to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique IDs.

For the ATT&CK Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the IDs obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mapping, retrieve the Tactic node(s) each is associated with via HAS_TACTIC, to identify the broad intrusion phases (e.g., Initial Access, Privilege Escalation, Lateral Movement) under which these techniques are classified.

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

gold_question: Which CAPEC patterns exploit weakness CWE-522, which ATT&CK techniques do they map to, and what mitigations apply?
note: schema words replaced with plain phrasing

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node representing CWE-522. Return the AttackPattern id, name, and description.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK. Return the entry_id (ATT&CK technique id) and the TaxonomyEntry details.
Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK ids supplied from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings (q2). Return technique name, id, and tactic.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation name and description.
For the Technique and SubTechnique nodes retrieved in q3, find all Mitigation nodes that have a MITIGATES relationship to them. Return mitigation name, id, and description.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

gold_question: Which CAPEC patterns exploit weakness CWE-522, which ATT&CK techniques do they map to, and what mitigations apply?
note: dash-fragment sentence shape

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node representing CWE-522. Return the AttackPattern nodes and their associated TaxonomyEntry nodes (MAPS_TO, taxonomy=ATTACK) so the ATT&CK entry_ids are available for the join.

Find all Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK entry_ids produced by the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry nodes (taxonomy=ATTACK) linked from the AttackPatterns in q1. Return the Technique/SubTechnique nodes with their names and IDs.
For the AttackPattern nodes identified in q1 (those exploiting CWE-522), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation names and descriptions.
For the Technique and SubTechnique nodes identified in q2, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES. Return mitigation names and descriptions.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node representing CWE-287 (Improper Authentication). Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs.
Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings in q2. Return their names, descriptions, and associated Tactic(s).
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its associated Mitigation nodes via the HAS_MITIGATION relationship. Return mitigation names and descriptions.
For the ATT&CK Technique and SubTechnique nodes identified in q3, retrieve all Mitigation nodes that have a MITIGATES relationship to them. Return mitigation names and descriptions.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000

gold_question: Which CAPEC patterns exploit weakness CWE-294, which ATT&CK techniques do they map to, and what mitigations apply?
note: schema words replaced with plain phrasing

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node with id CWE-294. Return the AttackPattern id, name, and description.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, returning the entry_id (ATT&CK technique id) and any mapping metadata.
Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK technique ids obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings in q2. Return id, name, and description.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes linked via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation id, name, and description.
For each Technique/SubTechnique identified in q3, retrieve all Mitigation nodes that have a MITIGATES relationship to them. Return mitigation id, name, and description.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

note: dash-fragment sentence shape

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to a Weakness node representing CWE-294, and for each such AttackPattern retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry entries (especially those with taxonomy=ATTACK) to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique IDs.

Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings (join on attack-technique-id), and for each matched technique/sub-technique retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES.
For the same set of AttackPatterns that exploit CWE-294 (identified in q1), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION to provide CAPEC-level defensive recommendations.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

For the ATT&CK Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the entry_ids from q2, retrieve their names, descriptions, and all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship (i.e., mitigations that address those techniques).

MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

note: paraphrased the name's idea, no id, name, or avoid words

plan.text: Find the AttackPattern that describes the practice of prepending decoy characters to a request so that input-validation filters let it through (e.g., filter evasion / input manipulation via leading characters), and retrieve its associated Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION.

Find the Technique or SubTechnique whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK entry_id declared in the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry (taxonomy=ATTACK) that the q1 AttackPattern MAPS_TO, to identify which ATT&CK method(s) the practice corresponds to.
Find all Mitigation nodes that MITIGATES the Technique or SubTechnique identified in q2, to enumerate ATT&CK-level defenses that help stop the practice.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

CAPEC-16 (Dictionary-based Password Attack): An attacker tries each of the words in a dictionary as passwords to gain access to the system via some user's account. If the password chosen by the user was a word within the dictionary, this attack will be successful (in the absence of other mitigations). This is a specific instance of the password brute forcing attack pattern. Dictionary Attacks differ from similar attacks such as Password Spraying (CAPEC-565) and Credential Stuffing (CAPEC-600), since they leverage unknown username/password combinations and don't care about inducing account lockouts.

CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)) has Abstraction: Standard; Likelihood_Of_Attack: High; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: Very High.

CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)): An adversary embeds malicious scripts in content that will be served to web browsers. The goal of the attack is for the target software, the client-side browser, to execute the script with the users' privilege level. An attack of this type exploits a programs' vulnerabilities that are brought on by allowing remote hosts to execute code and scripts. Web browsers, for example, have some simple security controls in place, but if a remote attacker is allowed to execute scripts (through injecting them in to user-generated content like bulletin boards) then these controls may be bypassed. Further, these attacks are very difficult for an end user to detect.

For each AttackPattern that maps to T1021 via a TaxonomyEntry (taxonomy=ATT&CK, entry_id=T1021), retrieve the Resource nodes connected to that AttackPattern via REQUIRES_RESOURCE. Return resource name and description.

For Technique T1021: (a) find DataComponent nodes reachable via DetectionStrategy -[DETECTS]-> Technique (reverse) then DetectionStrategy -[HAS_ANALYTIC]-> Analytic -[MONITORS]-> DataComponent; (b) find Software nodes connected to T1021 via the USES relationship. Return names and descriptions.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 10

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 200

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 200

plan.text: Retrieve the Valid Accounts technique (T1078) and all of its SubTechniques (e.g., T1078.001 Domain Accounts, T1078.002 Local Accounts, T1078.003 Cloud Accounts, T1078.004 Default), together with every Tactic each is associated with via HAS_TACTIC. claims: CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) description: In applications, particularly web applications, access to functionality is mitigated by an authorization framework. This framework maps Access Control Lists (ACLs) to elements of the application's functionality; particularly URL's for web apps. In the case that the administrator failed to specify an ACL for a particular element, an attacker may be able to access it with impunity. An attacker with the ability to access functionality not properly constrained by ACLs can obtain sensitive information and possibly compromise the entire application. Such an attacker can access resources that must be available only to users at a higher privilege level, can access management sections of the application, or can run queries for data that they otherwise not supposed to..

CAPEC-100 (Overflow Buffers) description: Buffer Overflow attacks target improper or missing bounds checking on buffer operations, typically triggered by input injected by an adversary. As a consequence, an adversary is able to write past the boundaries of allocated buffer regions in memory, causing a program crash or potentially redirection of execution as per the adversaries' choice..

CAPEC-101 (Server Side Include (SSI) Injection) description: An attacker can use Server Side Include (SSI) Injection to send code to a web application that then gets executed by the web server. Nonetheless, the attacker can conveniently gain access to sensitive files, such as password files, and execute shell commands..

CAPEC-62 (Cross Site Request Forgery) description: An attacker crafts malicious web links and distributes them (via web pages, email, etc.), typically in a targeted manner, hoping to induce users to click on the link and execute the malicious action against some third-party application. If successful, the action embedded in the malicious link will be processed and accepted by the targeted application with the users' privilege level. This type of attack leverages the persistence and implicit trust placed in user session cookies by many web applications today. In such an architecture, once the user authenticates to an application and a session cookie is created on the user's system, all following transactions for that session are authenticated using that cookie including potential actions initiated by an attacker and simply "riding" the existing session cookie..

CAPEC-621 (Analysis of Packet Timing and Sizes) description: An attacker may intercept and log encrypted transmissions for the purpose of analyzing metadata such as packet timing and sizes. Although the actual data may be encrypted, this metadata may reveal valuable information to an attacker. Note that this attack is applicable to VOIP data as well as application data, especially for interactive apps that require precise timing and low-latency (e.g. thin-clients)..

CAPEC-622 (Electromagnetic Side-Channel Attack) description: In this attack scenario, the attacker passively monitors electromagnetic emanations that are produced by the targeted electronic device as an unintentional side-effect of its processing. From these emanations, the attacker derives information about the data that is being processed (e.g. the attacker can recover cryptographic keys by monitoring emanations associated with cryptographic processing). This style of attack requires proximal access to the device, however attacks have been demonstrated at public conferences that work at distances of up to 10-15 feet. There have not been any significant studies to determine the maximum practical distance for such attacks. Since the attack is passive, it is nearly impossible to detect and the targeted device will continue to operate as normal after a successful attack..

CAPEC-623 (Compromising Emanations Attack) description: Compromising Emanations (CE) are defined as unintentional signals which an attacker may intercept and analyze to disclose the information processed by the targeted equipment. Commercial mobile devices and retransmission devices have displays, buttons, microchips, and radios that emit mechanical emissions in the form of sound or vibrations. Capturing these emissions can help an adversary understand what the device is doing..

CAPEC-624 (Hardware Fault Injection) description: The adversary uses disruptive signals or events, or alters the physical environment a device operates in, to cause faulty behavior in electronic devices. plan.text: Find all Techniques and SubTechniques that describe (a) acquiring or stealing credentials that belong to another user (Credential Access tactic), (b) using those valid credentials to authenticate to a system (Valid Accounts, T1078 and its sub-techniques), and (c) leveraging remote-access channels specifically RDP (T1021.001) or SSH (T1021.004) to gain a foothold. Return the technique names, IDs, parent tactics, and any sub-technique breakdowns.

For the techniques identified in q1 (credential-acquisition techniques, T1078 Valid Accounts and its sub-techniques, T1021 Remote Services with RDP and SSH sub-techniques), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return mitigation names, IDs, and descriptions of the defensive measures.

For the techniques identified in q1, retrieve all DetectionStrategy nodes connected via DETECTS, and for each DetectionStrategy retrieve its associated Analytic nodes (HAS_ANALYTIC) and the DataComponent log sources those analytics MONITORS. Return strategy names, analytic IDs, and monitored data components.

Find CAPEC AttackPattern nodes that describe (a) an attacker obtaining or guessing another user's credentials (e.g., credential theft, brute-force, credential stuffing), (b) using those valid credentials to authenticate to a system, and (c) exploiting remote-access channels such as RDP or SSH to gain a foothold. For each matching pattern, also retrieve its ExecutionStep nodes (HAS_EXECUTION_STEP) and any Indicator nodes (HAS_INDICATOR) that describe observable signs of the attack.

For the CAPEC AttackPattern nodes identified in q4, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION and any Prerequisite or Resource nodes that describe conditions or capabilities the attacker needs. Return mitigation descriptions, prerequisites, and required resources.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

plan.text: Find the AttackPatterns named 'Embedding Scripts within Scripts', 'Leverage Executable Code in Non-Executable Files', and 'Embed Virus into DLL'; for each, traverse MAPS_TO to TaxonomyEntry nodes whose taxonomy is ATTACK, and return the entry_id (ATT&CK technique id) for each mapping.
For each ATT&CK Technique or SubTechnique whose attack_id matches the ids produced by q1 (deduplicated union), retrieve the node and all Mitigation nodes reachable via the MITIGATES relationship.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Identify the Technique and SubTechnique nodes that correspond to each of these three adversary behaviors: (1) hiding one script inside another so it quietly executes as well, (2) sneaking runnable code into files not intended to execute code (e.g. image files, configuration files), (3) slipping malicious code into leftover padding or unused instruction space inside a compiled library binary. Return the matching Technique/SubTechnique nodes with their IDs and names.

For every Technique and SubTechnique identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship, so the combined set of ATT&CK countermeasures covering all three behaviors is returned.

Find AttackPattern nodes whose MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry (taxonomy=ATTACK) entry_id matches the ATT&CK technique IDs returned in q1, and for each such AttackPattern retrieve its Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION, to supplement the ATT&CK mitigations with CAPEC-level countermeasures.

plan.text: Find all TaxonomyEntry nodes (where taxonomy is ATT&CK) that are targets of MAPS_TO relationships originating from AttackPattern CAPEC-13 and AttackPattern CAPEC-640. Return each entry_id so the corresponding ATT&CK technique IDs can be resolved.

Retrieve all Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs supplied from the CAPEC mapping (the combined/union set from CAPEC-13 and CAPEC-640). For each matched technique or sub-technique, also retrieve every Mitigation node connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return technique IDs, names, and their associated mitigations.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

plan.text: Find the Technique or SubTechnique describing an adversary modifying environment variables (settings a running program reads from its environment, e.g. PATH, LD_PRELOAD) so the program's runtime behavior deviates from its intended purpose in favor of the attacker.

Find the Technique or SubTechnique describing an adversary injecting external code or instructions into a separate, already-running process's memory space, exploiting that process's failure to validate external writers, thereby gaining access to resources within that process's address space.
Retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES to the techniques identified in q1 (environment-variable manipulation) and q2 (process injection), to build the ATT&CK-side countermeasure set.

Find the AttackPattern describing manipulation of environment variables to alter a program's runtime behavior (attacker edits settings the program reads, causing it to deviate from intended behavior), and retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION to that pattern.
